    <title>Lee-Yang theorems for $q$-deformed oscillators and doubly-scaled SYK</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:52:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03624v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03624v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We show that the vacuum partition function of the $q$-deformed oscillator
  \[
  L_q(z):= \langle0|e^{zT_q}|0\rangle, \qquad T_q := \mathsf{a}_q + \mathsf{a}_q^*
  \] satisfies the Lee-Yang property, i.e., all zeros of $L_q$ lie on the imaginary line for all $q\in[-1, 1)$, proving the conjectures of Okuyama'23. Using the connection between $q$-deformed oscillators and the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) Hamiltonian in the doubly-scaled regime, we show that the annealed SYK partition function satisfies the Lee-Yang property in the thermodynamic limit, that is, all of its Fisher zeros are on the imaginary axis. As a result, we show that the quenched SYK partition function admits a zero-free strip of constant width with high probability, rigorously complementing the large$-k$ replica calculations of Zlokapa and Kiani'26.
  We show the imaginary-rootedness of $L_q$ by expressing $\varphi_q(z):= L_q(\mathbf{i} z)$ as a locally uniform limit of ``$q$-deformed'' matching polynomials and then showing that those $q$-deformed polynomials are real-rooted. This establishes that $\varphi_q$ is real-rooted, and in fact belongs to the \emph{Laguerre-Pólya} class. The real-rootedness of the $q$-deformed polynomials yields novel log-concavity relations on the \emph{$q$-deformed matching moments}
  \[M_\ell(q):= \sum_{π\in\mathcal{P}_2(2\ell)}q^{\operatorname{cr}(π)}.\]
  We show the real-rootedness of the $q$-deformed polynomials by using the Touchard--Riordan formula to derive a partial differential equation relating their $q$-derivatives to their $z$-derivatives, and then analyzing the resulting motion of their roots.</summary>

    <title>Thought-deciphering via hierarchical EEG-to-text alignment</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:52:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03623v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03623v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Communication is important for our well-being, but it can be impaired by disabilities, such as locked-in syndrome (LIS), cerebral palsy (CP), and dysarthria. Non-invasive brain-to-text brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a promising solution by providing an alternative communication pathway for people with communication disabilities. However, most recent breakthroughs have relied on large, cumbersome, and costly neuroimaging modalities, such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). Numerous studies have attempted decoding using the lighter and cheaper electroencephalography (EEG), but the results remain inferior compared to the other modalities. More importantly, we do not understand how these modalities are related to text at the letter, word, sentence, and higher semantic levels. Many prior studies have focused on decoding below the sentence level because it is considerably easier to design an experiment around phonemes, letters, and words. However, during communication, sentences play a much more important role than words and letters. This is because sentences carry information at such a high level that they can be understood even if some words and letters are missing. However, within sentence-level decoding, sentence classification is not as well investigated as sentence generation, making it difficult to decide whether a sentence should be retrieved or generated in the context of EEG-to-text decoding. This paper strives to investigate sentence-level EEG-to-text classification via a novel hierarchical alignment framework, where the main goal is to retrieve a read sentence using its context and EEG as inputs.</summary>

    <title>D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment Enables VLMs as Zero-Shot Robotic Reward Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:52:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03622v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03622v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold promise for zero-shot video task-progress estimation in robot learning, yet existing frameworks frequently suffer from confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed executions due to implicit success assumptions or relative temporal ranking designs. Naive prompting of frontier models collapses into a binary success detector that fails to capture nuanced, non-linear progress and failures. While post-training approaches can mitigate this through explicit training, they demand expensive real-world robotics data and require computationally intensive post-training for every individual base model. To resolve these limitations, we introduce D&A (Describe & Assess): our approach decouples progress estimation into an objective, task-grounded textual description of scene dynamics followed by an assessment phase using explicit rubrics. By compelling the VLM to synthesize an explicit, text-based definition of absolute success before scoring, the framework anchors evaluations to an external, global criterion rather than the video's internal timeline. Empirical results demonstrate that our method calibrates zero-shot estimates and mitigates confirmation bias, providing fine-grained, partial progress metrics that accurately penalize failed executions while correctly interpolating successful runs. Being purely prompt-based, D&A generalizes across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks---matching or surpassing post-trained reward models---and its reward estimates enable efficient downstream reinforcement learning.</summary>

    <title>Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:51:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03618v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03618v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A model is only half of an AI agent system. The other half is the inference strategy: the reasoning procedure that turns model calls into a response. Today that second half is written by hand, and the experience of building one strategy never carries to the next. We introduce Strategist, a meta-agent that evolves inference strategies across tasks. Each strategy is written as a blueprint,executable code that other strategies can reuse, and together the blueprints form a library. Given a task and a small development set, Strategist retrieves related blueprints, writes candidate strategies, tests them on real samples, and revises them from the results. Every candidate then enters the library, so later tasks build on earlier discoveries. On 30 benchmarks, Strategist beats the strongest baseline on 24 and matches its average accuracy (74.7% vs.74.0%) at 39% lower inference cost. Its strategies also transfer to unseen tasks and other models without further search. The part of an AI system that is not improved on its own now does.</summary>

    <title>Tracing the Scientific Discovery Capacity of LLMs to Their Training Data</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:50:54Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03617v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) show growing promise for scientific discovery, yet basic questions remain about what enables reliable discovery. How can we trace the scientific discovery capacity of LLMs to their training data? We study this question as one of missing probability mass and develop a theoretical account in which monofacts-the facts observed once during training-set the discovery capacity. In materials science and regulatory genomics, we directly manipulate monofact rates in training sets and find that more monofacts consistently yield more discoveries across two open-weight model families, sampling strategies, and reasoning budgets. Further experiments show the relationship cannot be explained by training-set diversity alone and can transfer across scientific domains when paired with in-domain data. Together, our results identify monofact rate in training data as a key factor governing discoveries in language models.</summary>

    <summary>Evaluating a generative model on all queries from all available benchmark tasks is prohibitively expensive. As such, models are often evaluated on different subsets of tasks and/or different subsets of queries from a given task. The resulting collection of responses and the corresponding (model, task) score matrix are sparse and unpaired. In this paper, we introduce the Product Kernel Perspective Space (PKPS), a collection of low-dimensional representations of models based on their embedded responses. PKPS generalizes existing methods for representing black-box generative models by comparing responses to similar -- rather than just identical -- queries and is therefore able to utilize sparse and unpaired information. Theoretically, we show that benchmark prediction using PKPS is query-efficient relative to methods that only use information from dense and paired portions of the evaluation data. Empirically, we show that PKPS-based methods outperform baselines on benchmark prediction across two large benchmark suites.</summary>

    <title>Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches</title>

    <summary>Increased computing power has transformed computational science and improved predictive capabilities for complex systems, but many phenomena still exceed current simulation capabilities or require rapid evaluations for fast design iterations. Closure models address this challenge by approximating unresolved effects in reduced or incomplete dynamical systems. Data-driven closures offer a flexible mechanism for improving model accuracy and applicability, but approaches that embed the closure within a computational model for construction and training phases can be computationally expensive and cause numerical instabilities in the computational model during training. To avoid the challenges posed by embedded approaches, staged approaches to closure-model learning have been developed. The first stage uses data assimilation to infer state and closure trajectories from observations. The second stage trains a machine learning closure model offline using the assimilated data, thereby avoiding repeated simulator calls during training. In this work, we investigate the cost and accuracy tradeoffs between embedded and staged data-driven closure modeling approaches for a synthetic epidemiological SIQR model with a nonlinear state-dependent quarantine closure. The results illustrate a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off: for this exemplar, embedded training provides the strongest average accuracy, while the staged approach yields comparable qualitative behavior with a moderate increase in error, substantially fewer model evaluations, and improved optimization robustness.</summary>

    <title>DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:41:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03601v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control.</summary>

    <title>Four Bridges: Measuring Deception Propensity in a Multi-Agent Game</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:40:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03600v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03600v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>AI agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact and coordinate with other agents, yet honesty is mostly measured in single-turn, single-agent benchmarks that pressure the model to deceive. We study deception that emerges in multi-agent interaction without any instruction to deceive. We introduce Kradle, a platform for evaluating AI models, and Four Bridges, an information asymmetry game in which four agents distribute across four rooms: one is the death room, the others hold food worth more if not shared. One agent, the informed agent, knows which room is the death room and can withhold or disclose that information. We evaluate eight frontier models as the informed agent. Deceptive behavior appears in every model and in 73% of all runs (6% to 100% per model), and does not decrease with capability tier within a model family. When the informed agent does disclose, the warning is often challenged, and agents that challenge it enter the death room twice as often as those that do not. Telling all agents that one of them knows the death room collapses deception in six of eight models; telling the informed agent that the room is permanently fatal moves only one. On an open-weight model, an honesty steering vector reduces deception to 0% and adversarial honesty training to 6%. The platform and game provide a testbed for measuring deceptive behavior and comparing interventions.</summary>

    <title>Should We Combine Our Data? Algorithms and Limits for Privately Assessing Data Sharing</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:40:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03599v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03599v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In this paper, we study when two parties should pool their data to train a machine learning model. Two agents, Alice and Bob, each hold a sensitive labeled dataset and want to train a classifier from a given hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$. Even when each party's dataset can be perfectly classified on its own, the two parties may follow conflicting labeling standards or have selection biases that affect their features and label sets, such that no single classifier in $\mathcal{H}$ fits their combined data. Before committing to data sharing, Alice and Bob therefore want to test whether a single classifier in $\mathcal{H}$ can jointly fit both datasets---without revealing their individual data points to one another.
  We formalize this problem from a learning-theoretic viewpoint via $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}$, the minimum \emph{number of mistakes} made by any hypothesis in $\mathcal{H}$ on their pooled data. Through interactive communication, the agents must distinguish $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}=0$ (compatible datasets) from $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}\geq t$ (conflicting datasets) under pure $\varepsilon$-two-party differential privacy. A trusted curator could do this with $t=O(1/\varepsilon)$, and we ask how small $t$ can be without one. For thresholds on the real line over a domain of size $m$, we show that the optimal $t$ is $\tildeΘ(\log\log m/\varepsilon)$, exponentially smaller than the $Θ(\log m/\varepsilon)$ samples needed to privately learn thresholds, even with a curator. For halfspaces in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the dependence on $m$ jumps to $\log(m)$: we give a protocol with $t=\tilde{O}(d^3\log m/\varepsilon)$ and show that some domains require $t=Ω(d\log(m/d)/\varepsilon)$.</summary>

    <title>Structured Visual Landscape: Generating Preferred Representations in Biological and Artificial Neural Networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:39:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03597v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03597v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Understanding how neurons respond to visual stimulus is an important question in both deep learning and neuroscience. It has significant implications for enhancing the interpretability of black-box artificial neural networks and for understanding the visual representation in the human brain. We propose a structured visual representations landscape and design an activation-based prior that allows us to effectively regularize the landscape with activations from brain regions or neural network units. Our model Vis-Lens integrates a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model into an image generation framework. It enables the generation of natural, realistic preferred images by directly modifying the activation-regularized latent codes without per-image iterative optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on both artificial neural networks and human visual cortex using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. Our framework improves activation modulation and image realism compared with a recent state-of-the-art method for generating preferred visual representations of these neural targets.</summary>

    <title>Spacetime Emergence in the Memory of a Learning Agent</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:39:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03596v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03596v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We show that the causal structure of spacetime can emerge within the memory of a learning agent performing a quantum information task. We train a model-based reinforcement-learning agent to maximize the quantum mutual information between localized quantum probes interacting with a quantum field in Minkowski spacetime, without directly providing it with information regarding the spacetime metric or causal structure. In learning to accomplish this task, the reinforcement-learning agent constructs an internal predictive model whose planner develops the characteristic null structure of spacetime, allowing us to reconstruct the causal structure of the Minkowski metric with high accuracy. Within this task, spacetime geometry is obtained from an agent's successful predictions and actions, providing a first step toward showing that spacetime concepts emerge from operational quantum experience.</summary>

    <title>DynaSolver: A Neural Operator for Autoregressive 4D Flow Prediction with Dynamic Boundaries</title>

    <summary>Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD), but most are designed for static geometries and are not equipped to model unsteady flows induced by continuously moving boundaries. We study dynamic-boundary 4D CFD prediction for articulated moving geometries and introduce RoboCFD-4D, a temporally resolved robotic CFD benchmark spanning diverse morphologies and flow conditions. To address the computational and autoregressive challenges of this setting, we propose DynaSolver, a neural operator that explicitly conditions on boundary evolution and causal flow history. DynaSolver employs an efficient physical-token formulation that amortizes point-to-token projection across the operator stack, substantially reducing repeated point-space spatio-temporal computation while retaining accurate point-level reconstruction. We further introduce Replay-Augmented Parallel Training, which exposes the model to autoregressively generated histories while preserving parallel dense supervision, narrowing the gap between ground-truth-conditioned training and autoregressive rollout. Experiments on RoboCFD-4D show that DynaSolver achieves the best full-rollout accuracy among a broad range of learned CFD surrogates, with its advantage increasing as rollout proceeds, indicating substantially reduced autoregressive error accumulation. Project page: https://made-gpt.github.io/DynaSolver-ProjectPage.</summary>

    <title>Evaluating Uncertainty Calibration in Probabilistic Time Series Foundation Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:34:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03592v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03592v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are increasingly used for probabilistic forecasting across diverse domains, yet the reliability of their uncertainty estimates remains poorly understood. In this work, we study uncertainty calibration in probabilistic TSFMs from a broader methodological and empirical perspective. We introduce a taxonomy of how TSFMs represent predictive uncertainty and develop a fine-grained evaluation framework for calibration in multi-horizon forecasting that distinguishes pooled, horizon-wise, and stronger conditional notions of calibration. Using this framework, we conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation of popular TSFMs across diverse datasets and show that current models exhibit distinct and systematic patterns of miscalibration that standard metrics often obscure. We further analyze common post-hoc recalibration methods and characterize which forms of calibration they can improve and which tend to persist. Our results provide practical guidance for evaluating and improving uncertainty calibration in TSFMs and highlight important limitations of current practice.</summary>

    <title>A Scaling Theory of Multi-Epoch Pretraining: Late-Time Overfitting and Ensembling</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:34:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03590v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>In the near future language model pretraining will become bound by total data rather than total compute. Such a regime requires revisiting scaling laws and scaling law theory. Motivated by prior works that have found utility in ensembling, we study how the number of training epochs and ensemble size jointly shape generalization when training data are fixed. In language-model experiments on FineWeb, logit averaging reduces late-training deterioration, delays optimal stopping, and can outperform wider or deeper single models at matched parameter-token budgets over a common training horizon. To analyze this interaction between data reuse and ensembling, we derive a dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for multi-epoch stochastic gradient descent in power-law random-feature ensembles, tracking error correlations across epochs and models. Ensembling reduces the prediction variance responsible for late-time growth in expected test error, changing the optimal stopping time. We use these stopping times to derive compute-allocation laws at fixed data and individual model sizes. Under this allocation, ensemble size grows with compute at least as fast as training time per member, while excess test loss above the limiting loss decreases as a power of compute.</summary>

    <title>FedReady: Bounded Agents for Federation Formation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:32:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03586v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Federated learning (FL) runtimes standardize aggregation and deployment, but each new study still requires federation formation: selecting task-eligible sites and preparing their local data and task code for federated training or analysis. This preparation recurs when the target changes, while raw records and site-private mappings are excluded from cross-site FL messages. We present FedReady, a system that performs federation formation with bounded LLM agents. Agents propose shared contracts, local adapters, and task code; the runtime owns workflow state and accepts artifacts only after checks tied to their digests. Candidate site discovery prioritizes recall; local eligibility verification checks task support before site admission. Once participating sites and artifacts are fixed, conventional federated training or analysis proceeds without readiness agents. Across 39 simulated retinal sites and four tasks, discovery reaches recall 1.00 at precision 0.65; local eligibility verification removes all 17 false positives without losing an eligible site-task pair. The participating sites supply 45,575 task-record instances and complete four 100-round jobs, including one with a runtime-generated contract. Across ten patient cohorts, preparation supports seven patient populations and holds endpoints at three sources as unsupported. Comparison with manually prepared reference populations and analysis (the manual reference) gives a maximum survival-curve difference of 0.001133. We also analyze 19 development failures, targeted classification ablations, and standalone and heterogeneous agent configurations. These results establish the feasibility of task-specific data preparation before ordinary FL training or analysis.</summary>

    <title>Single-pass stochastic cooling for electron microscopy</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:31:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03581v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03581v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Scientific applications of free electrons, such as in electron microscopes and particle accelerators, are limited by the brightness of available electron sources. Accelerators can use phase space cooling to surpass these source limitations, whereas electron microscopes can only rely on particle filtering to increase beam coherence at the cost of reduced brightness. We show that strong electron-light coupling in nanophotonic structures makes it possible to achieve single-pass stochastic cooling inside an electron microscope for a lossless improvement of longitudinal emittance. This approach is laser-free and compatible with normal CW operation of electron microscopes. We derive a fully quantum mechanical model of stochastic cooling valid in the strong coupling regime, finding an analytic asymptotic formula for the optimal cooled energy spread $σ_{E_f}\simeq0.88(\hbarω)^{2/3}σ_{E_0}^{1/3}$, with $\hbar ω$ the cooling photon energy and $σ_{E_0}$ the initial energy spread. Numerical simulations confirm that the energy spread reduction is reflected in an increase in the purity of the electron's quantum state and a reduction of the longitudinal phase space area. Our work paves a path towards even brighter beams for electron microscopy, promising higher image quality, enhanced spectral resolution, and a route to reaching fundamental quantum limits on electron beam phase space area.</summary>

    <title>Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:30:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03577v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale. We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients. When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines. Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory. Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.</summary>

    <title>BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:27:22Z</updated>

    <summary>Exemplar-free continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers increasingly relies on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), yet prevailing methods govern the low-rank update space through strict subspace isolation. By projecting each incoming task into the approximate null space of historical token activations, isolation-based learners equate any cross-task feature overlap with catastrophic interference. We show that this orthogonality premise induces a structural bottleneck we term \emph{spectral starvation}: when down-projection bases are locked before task optimization, the gradient norm reaching the trainable up-projection is upper-bounded by the energy of current-task features captured by the chosen basis. Because natural visual tasks share low- and mid-level covariance structure, historical null tails contain barely $5.5\%$ of incoming task variance, starving new-class plasticity while blocking positive consolidation along shared directions. We propose BISECT (Bilevel Spectral Decomposition), a continual LoRA framework that partitions a fixed rank-$r$ budget into two orthogonal functional blocks: an invariant carrier spanned by the dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix, and a novelty complement extracted via generalized Rayleigh whitening followed by orthogonal complement projection. After single-task training, BISECT folds both blocks back into the frozen backbone using a closed-form precision gate that scales each rank-1 invariant atom by its current-to-joint Rayleigh ratio while preserving novelty atoms at unit gain. Across eight incremental settings on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and DomainNet, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines with zero extra inference parameters or FLOPs, and remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.</summary>

    <title>Quantum Private Information Retrieval on Forests</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:19:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03558v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>We consider the problem of graph private information retrieval (PIR) in the quantum setting. We focus on a specific type of graphs, namely the forest graphs. A forest graph is a union of disjoint trees. We consider the quantum setting where all the servers share an entangled state. Each server is allowed to send only one qudit per retrieval round. We design a scheme for the forest graphs that achieves the rate of $\frac{3}{N}$. The scheme uses a GHZ state as the initial entangled state between the servers prior to the scheme initiation. We compare our scheme with the only work done in the literature that considered the quantum setting of graph PIR. We show that our scheme is more efficient in this setting. We derive the quantum capacity for the case of $G=3K_2$, which is equal to $4/6$. $G=3K_2$ is a special case of the forest graph. We design a scheme that is specialized for this graph, achieving a rate equal to $4/6$ and provide the corresponding matching upper bound, establishing it as the capacity.</summary>

    <title>PlantVLM-Edge: Quantized Vision-Language Models for On-Device Crop Health Diagnosis</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:19:19Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03557v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03557v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is essential for sustainable agricultural production, yet accurate diagnosis often requires expert knowledge that is not readily available. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, and natural-language interaction, creating new opportunities for intelligent crop health assessment. However, deploying VLMs on resource-constrained devices remains challenging due to their substantial computational and memory requirements. This paper presents PlantVLM-Edge, a quantized vision-language framework for conversational crop health diagnosis that can run entirely on resource-constrained edge devices. PlantVLM-Edge combines agricultural domain adaptation, post-training quantization, and on-device serving with an offline chat interface, allowing growers to ask open-ended questions and receive diagnoses, symptom explanations, and management guidance without cloud connectivity. The framework is backbone-agnostic: we validate it with two different VLM types with varying scale and architecture (Qwen3-VL-2B and LLaVA-1.5-7B), four quantization schemes, and two diagnostic domains (plant diseases and insect pests), and we deploy all variants on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Eight-bit quantization affects answer quality minimally relative to the full-precision model, and 4-bit activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) retains 98.6% of full-precision answer quality on both domains while reducing the weight memory of the 2B backbone by 49%. In its most compact form, PlantVLM-Edge requires 2.01 GiB of weight memory, returns its first token in about 0.12 s, and completes a 64-token diagnostic response in 0.78 s. These results demonstrate that timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is practical on edge devices, providing a foundation for next-generation crop monitoring and decision support systems.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03555v1</id>
    <title>MCP Tool Poisoning in Agentic AI Frameworks: A Cross-Framework Measurement Study</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:17:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03555v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03555v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets agentic AI frameworks connect language models to external tool providers, but it carries attacker-controlled content (tool descriptions, schema fields, and response data) into model context without validation. Prior benchmarks measure model compliance with poisoned instructions without confirming real execution. We present the first cross-framework measurement of MCP tool poisoning with real tool execution. A 25-class root-cause taxonomy unifies prior classifications, and the open-source tool mcpvenom drives a 9,720-cell susceptibility matrix across 12 frameworks, 18 models, and 45 attack scenarios, with a dual oracle that confirms exfiltration via canary HTTP receipt. The overall attack success rate is 22.9% (2,113 vulnerable cells). Of these, 64.9% dispatch an attacker tool call, 23.0% contact the attacker endpoint, and 12.1% verifiably exfiltrate a secret. Resistance is model-level: nine core frameworks cluster within 23 to 26% (chi-squared = 3.30, p = 0.91), and no framework implements intentional defense. Incidental framework properties mitigate in specific cases, and a regex description scanner rejects 20 of 45 scenarios at a 7.2% false-positive rate, so metadata scanning alone is a partial control. Model ASR ranges from 0.4% to 49.7%. Claude Opus 4.8 is vulnerable in 8 of 530 cells while issuing 223 explicit refusals. A code-level audit finds no intentional defense across twelve frameworks, and all five coordinated disclosures across four vendors were rejected.</summary>

    <title>Nonparametric Intensity Estimation for Covariate-Driven Poisson Processes Using Deep Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:14:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03552v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03552v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We consider nonparametric maximum likelihood estimation of the intensity function of a Poisson process, allowing the intensity to depend on observed covariates. Such models describe how event rates vary with external conditions, including conditions under which the intensity becomes arbitrarily small or vanishes. However, risk analysis based on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence typically requires the true intensity to be bounded away from zero, a restrictive assumption in applications. We develop a unified approach that avoids this assumption and derive an oracle inequality for the covariate-averaged Hellinger distance between the true intensity and the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE). As an application of the oracle inequality, we establish convergence rates for NPMLEs based on deep neural networks (DNNs). Our results show that, as in nonparametric regression, the ability of DNNs to capture underlying structure leads to improved convergence rates. Specifically, DNN-based NPMLEs mitigate the curse of dimensionality when the true intensity has a compositional structure and automatically adapt to a low-dimensional Riemannian manifold structure of the event space. For intensity functions with a compositional structure, DNN-based NPMLEs achieve nearly minimax-optimal convergence rates without explicitly incorporating this structure into the network architecture. Simulations demonstrate that DNN-based estimators outperform kernel estimators in most settings, while manifold kernels remain competitive in some designs. Finally, we analyze stimulus-evoked neural spiking using data from the Allen Brain Observatory Visual Coding Neuropixels project. DNN-based NPMLEs provide better out-of-sample performance than a conditional kernel estimator, as evaluated by held-out log-likelihood.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03551v1</id>
    <title>Can LLM Agents Be Forward-Deployed Engineers? Requirement Discovery and Delivery for Enterprise Text-to-SQL</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:13:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03551v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03551v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>LLM coding agents can increasingly automate model post-training, but whether they can act as forward-deployed engineer (FDE) agents, discovering customer requirements and turning them into deployment decisions, remains unclear. We study this on a real enterprise text-to-SQL engagement: a simulated customer, grounded in the real use case's requirements, starts with an ambiguous request. An agent must discover acceptance criteria, data permissions, and hardware constraints in the discovery phase, then plan and execute a post-training recipe in the delivery phase. Across 15 models, the strongest discover over 80% of withheld requirements and open-weight models discover 40-50%; in the delivery phase, only 25% of runs across eight coding-agent configurations pass all acceptance criteria. We identify four bottlenecks in this engagement: (1) incomplete discovery, with 40% of withheld requirements missing or misrepresented; (2) unreliable execution; (3) underused compute budgets and a lack of systematic comparisons across base models and post-training methods; and (4) benchmark accuracy does not guarantee production readiness. We suggest human review of discovered requirements, monitoring of the agent's plan during execution, and an explicit experiment-environment specification covering hardware, budget scope, and production checks.</summary>

    <title>Unifying entanglement and nonclassicality via the Narcowich-Wigner spectrum</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:06:17Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03544v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03544v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Entanglement and nonclassicality are two fundamental features of quantum mechanics which serve as resources in quantum information processing tasks and are tightly connected by two-mode mixing. In this work, we show that the connection between entanglement and nonclassicality extends well beyond the two-mode mixing setting by considering the case of arbitrary multimode Gaussian evolutions. Using the Narcowich-Wigner spectrum as our main technical tool to quantify single-mode phase-space nonclassicality, we derive sufficient conditions for a single-mode state to generate NPT entanglement after a multimode Gaussian unitary evolution, which both tighten and generalize existing criteria. As an application, we obtain simple single-mode protocols for quantitatively testing the entanglement structure of multimode quantum states over arbitrary bipartitions. Our results identify the Narcowich-Wigner spectrum as a powerful tool for investigating fundamental properties of bosonic quantum states.</summary>

    <title>Can LLM Agents Improve Imperfect Earth System Model Parameterizations?</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:05:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03543v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03543v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Earth system models (ESMs) rely on parameterizations to represent unresolved processes such as convection, cloud microphysics, and turbulence. However, translating advances in physical understanding into stable, validated parameterizations and integrating them into ESMs often takes years. Agentic AI could accelerate this process and enable more systematic exploration of design choices. Using warm-rain collision-coalescence as a test case, we evaluate agents' ability to synthesize scientific literature, reimplement published bulk parameterizations, and propose new functional forms as differentiable JAX code. We compare conventional parameterizations, data-driven emulators, and agent-generated closures against high-fidelity superdroplet simulations, repeating unattended experiments across ten language models. With expert guidance or iterative feedback, agents produced executable, differentiable, mass-conserving code, although unattended performance depended strongly on the scheme and language model. Iterative feedback lowered median rollout error for eight of ten models. Retuned physical schemes matched or outperformed many learned parameterizations at substantially lower computational cost, but two of 100 unattended agent-generated closures achieved slightly lower rain-mass error than the most accurate retuned scheme on held-out simulations.</summary>

    <title>Variational Functional Neural Networks (vfNN)</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:04:46Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03542v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03542v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We present a variational functional neural network (vfNN) algorithm that optimizes physically motivated continuum functionals in integral form (e.g., Lagrangian, Hamiltonian, or free energy) to find the states of a system. That way, vfNN bypasses solving the equations of motion (a.k.a. the Euler-Lagrange equations), which are in the form of differential equations. To this end, our approach is fundamentally different from conventional physics-informed neural networks (PINN) that solve differential equations by minimizing a phenomenological loss function involving higher order derivatives and ad hoc weight factors. In contrast, vfNN merely evaluates lower order derivatives of the generating functional and replaces the weight factors with rigorous physical scales. This also fundamentally changes the loss landscape, and the desired solutions may become unstable. For this emergent nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a quasi-Newton optimization algorithm with simulated annealing that converges to the solutions of the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations of the functional regardless of their stability properties. Our simulations using vfNN give accurate results for benchmark systems governed by linear or nonlinear ordinary differential equations.</summary>

    <title>An Agentic Framework for Automated Power System Studies and Grid Connection Assessment</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T18:00:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03534v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03534v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Connecting new generation and demand to the grid depends on two scarce skills: checking applications against a large, changing body of regulation, and running the network studies that decide where and how a project connects. We present Grid Agents, an AI system that brings both together, and the methodology we use to evaluate it. The Grid Ontology is its knowledge system. It represents the regulation, standards and engineering knowledge that grid work depends on, makes it searchable, and evolves as the agents learn from use. Every answer drawn from it rests on evidence the agents cite. Grid Studio is an agent system specialised for power-system engineering. It works in its own engineering environment with domain tools and a study framework, draws on the Grid Ontology, and relies on established solvers for every number it reports. In both, engineers make the decisions. We bring eight published power-system benchmark families, previously scattered across separate papers, into one suite of 519 tasks, and we verify not only each answer but the work behind it, by replaying the agent's tool calls. The Grid Ontology cites the right regulatory evidence more often than a general coding agent or retrieval pipelines, leads on LegalBench-RAG and ranks first on the public leaderboards of the Enterprise RAG Challenge and ViDoRe V3. Grid Studio scores highest on the 519 power-system tasks and is the fastest of all the systems we compare, both by a statistically significant margin. With an optimiser in the loop, its reinforcement packages cost 33-67% less on average than those the agent designs alone.</summary>

    <title>Contrastive Adapter Training and Consensus Knowledge Distillation for Multi-Source-Free Domain Adaptation in Skin Cancer Diagnosis</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T17:58:16Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03528v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03528v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Skin cancer diagnosis, particularly differentiating melanoma from benign nevi, is challenging due to the visual similarity between lesions. Although convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers (ViTs) have shown promising performance, their effectiveness often deteriorates on data from heterogeneous clinical sources. Conventional domain adaptation methods address domain shift but require access to source data during adaptation, which is often infeasible due to privacy regulations. Multi-source-free unsupervised domain adaptation (MSFDA) addresses this limitation by leveraging multiple labeled source domains to generalize to an unlabeled target domain without requiring access to source data. However, existing MSFDA methods rely on full backbone fine-tuning, leading to catastrophic forgetting and overfitting on small clinical datasets, and address domain shift at the aggregation stage without establishing a shared domain-invariant feature space. Furthermore, their reliance on hard pseudo-labels or confidence-weighted aggregation introduces noisy supervision signals under domain shift. To address these limitations, we propose CAT-CKD, consisting of two components: (1) contrastive adapter training (CAT), which trains lightweight ConvPass adapters within a frozen ViT backbone using supervised contrastive learning (SCL) to establish a shared domain-invariant feature space before source-specific model training, and (2) consensus knowledge distillation (CKD), which aggregates logits from multiple source models into a consensus supervisory signal and adapts a student model on unlabeled target data using KL divergence. Experiments on five publicly available skin lesion datasets show that CAT-CKD achieves an average AUROC of 86.1%, outperforming existing MSFDA methods while requiring only 4.3M trainable parameters. The code is available at https://github.com/A-Abedi/CAT_CKD.</summary>

    <title>Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T17:57:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03526v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03526v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.</summary>

    <title>Grading the Unannotated: Insights from the WorkRB Skill Extraction Challenge at RecSys-HR 2026</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T17:57:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03525v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03525v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Skill extraction benchmarks score models against a few human-annotated positives and treat every other skill in the vocabulary as equally wrong. At the scale of ESCO (13,939 skills) this binary view can reward models that rank the annotated positive high for the wrong reason, and hides semantically nonsensical predictions. The WorkRB Challenge at RecSys-HR 2026 replaces it with graded relevance: every candidate skill in a model's ranking window carries a 0 to 4 grade, and the leaderboard scores nDCG@100 against these grades. Since ternary judgements proved too coarse for objective annotation, relevance is decomposed into a cascade of four binary questions (same domain, activity mentioned, right granularity, replacement of a gold positive) that a smaller LLM judge can answer reliably; the labels are validated with blind human and frontier-model re-annotation. This paper documents the annotation methodology, the construction of five benchmark datasets (four with vacancy sentences as queries, one with lexically distant skill surface forms), the validation of the LLM cascade, and insights from the submissions. The field converged on multi-stage retrieve-and-rerank pipelines, whose gains come from clearing nonsense out of the ranking window rather than finding more positives: at the top of the leaderboard, the graded ordering is uncorrelated with what binary evaluation would have said. Graded labels expose much bigger gaps between top submissions and baselines than binary evaluation does, and show that semantic-understanding skill recommendation is still wide open. The clear next direction is bringing efficiency back: every submitted system we could size uses at least 42x, typically several hundred times, more parameters than the baselines it beats.</summary>

For enrolled subjects, clinical and laboratory evaluations will be performed and reported at different time points:

* Early (4-6 weeks after treatment start)
* Midtime (8-11 weeks after treatment start)
* Late (13-18 weeks after treatment start)
* At the occurrence of immune-related adverse events (irAEs), clinical and laboratory evaluation will be performed at two principal time points:

  * For the 1st time of any grade 1 or 2 irAE if the subject developed it.
  * For the 1st time of any grade 3 or 4 irAE if the subject developed it.","detailedDescription":"Advances in treating patients with immunotherapy has dramatically changed cancer morbidity and mortality. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI), alone or combined with other drugs, are currently used both as standard of care or in experimental settings for various cancers. Currently, ICI treatment induces objective clinical responses in 20-40% of patients, which varies by tumour type. A significant risk of immune-related adverse events (irAE) is also associated with ICI treatment, including the onset of autoimmune diseases. While the incidence of irAE is highly variable and influenced by many factors, phase I and II trials reported rates from 10% to 80% for any grade irAE while an irAE of grade 3 or higher was observed in 2.5% to 18% of subjects. Despite the fact that older adults represent the growing majority of patients diagnosed with cancer, the efficacy and toxicity of ICI in older patients, alone or in combination with other agents, remains controversial. Presently, the specific immune mechanism(s) driving irAE are unknown and biomarkers that predict their onset, particularly high-grade irAE, are urgently needed. The identification of predictive clinical, laboratory and immunological biomarkers (blood and tissue) for toxicity will more accurately identify and quantify patients who are at risk for ICI therapy. 1. Male or female participants aged ≥18 years at the time of screening
2. Recipient of an hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)
3. The disease indication for which the participant required HSCT must be in remission
4. Newly diagnosed acute graft-versus-host disease (GvHD), including lower Gastrointestinal (GI) involvement (modified International Bone Marrow Transplant Registry \[IBMTR\] Severity Stage 1 to 4 \[\>500 mL diarrhea/day\]), with or without other organ system involvement.
5. Willing to undergo or must have had a lower GI biopsy within 7 days of informed consent to confirm GI GvHD. Biopsy results are not needed to initiate treatment; however, if biopsy results are not consistent with aGvHD, treatment with GLASSIA will be discontinued.
6. Participants must be receiving systemic corticosteroids. Treatment with methylprednisolone/systemic steroids must have been initiated within 72 hours prior to the first dose of study treatment after enrollment
7. Evidence of myeloid engraftment (absolute neutrophil count ≥0.5 x 10\^9/L)
8. Lower GI GvHD manifested by diarrhea must have other causes of diarrhea ruled out (eg, negative for Clostridium difficile or cytomegalovirus \[CMV\] infection or oral magnesium administration)
9. Karnofsky Performance Score ≥50%
10. If female of childbearing potential, participant presents with a negative blood pregnancy test
11. Females of childbearing potential with a fertile male sexual partner must agree to employ adequate contraception for the duration of the study.
12. Males must use adequate contraception and must not donate sperm for the duration of the study.
13. Participant is willing and able to comply with the requirements of the protocol

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Participant with manifestations of chronic GvHD
2. Participant with acute/chronic GvHD overlap syndrome
3. Participant whose GvHD developed after donor lymphocyte infusion
4. Participant with myocardial infarction within 6 months prior to enrollment or New York Heart Association Class III or IV heart failure, uncontrolled angina, severe uncontrolled ventricular arrhythmias or electrocardiographic evidence of acute ischemia or active conduction system abnormalities. Prior to the first dose of study treatment, any electrocardiogram (ECG) abnormality at screening must be documented by the investigator as not medically relevant
5. Participant with evidence of recurrent malignancy
6. Participant with veno-occlusive disease (ie, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome)
7. Participant receiving GvHD treatment other than continued prophylaxis (eg, cyclosporine and/or mycophenolate mofetil, etc) or corticosteroid therapy. In addition, a participant who received the first dose of corticosteroid therapy for acute GvHD with lower GI involvement more than 72 hours before the first dose of study treatment is not eligible for the study
8. Participant with severe sepsis involving at least 1 organ failure
9. Participant who is seropositive or positive in the nucleic acid test for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
10. Participant with active hepatitis B or C
11. Participant has participated in another clinical study involving an investigational product (IP) or investigational device within 30 days prior to enrollment or is scheduled to participate in another clinical study involving an IP or investigational device during the course of this study
12. If female, participant is pregnant or lactating at the time of enrollment, or has plans to become pregnant during the study
13. Participant with a serious medical or psychiatric illness likely to interfere with participation in the study
14. Group 2 will use the app almost every day for 4 weeks.","detailedDescription":"Mental health concerns across the United States have increased substantially, affecting individuals across age groups, geographic regions, and socioeconomic backgrounds. Emerging adults demonstrate the highest prevalence of mental health conditions among adult populations, while simultaneously exhibiting the lowest rates of treatment utilization. Barriers to treatment for this population include limited affordability, accessibility, availability, and acceptability of mental health services.

Digital mental health interventions have demonstrated effectiveness across a range of outcomes, including symptom reduction, self-management, and well-being enhancement. Smartphone-based applications, in particular, have been evaluated as tools to integrate mental health support through scalable and accessible technologies. Such applications may offer features including guided self-help activities, mindfulness practices, journaling, mood tracking, psychoeducational content, and location-based resources for mental health services.

Following the COVID-19 pandemic, mental health challenges among U.S. college students have intensified, with documented impacts on academic performance and overall functioning. These challenges are further exacerbated by stigma, financial constraints, and limited access to campus-based or community mental health services, particularly for students from historically marginalized backgrounds.

In response to these needs, Penn State Behrend's Virtual/Augmented Reality (VAR) Lab developed the Landing Place mental health app, a free digital intervention designed to support mental wellness among college students in the Erie region. The application was developed with an emphasis on usability, privacy, and accessibility, and is tailored to the developmental and contextual needs of young adults. Planned future iterations of the application aim to extend its use to additional populations, such as survivors of domestic violence.

The Landing Place app incorporates artificial intelligence, supported features and evidence-based therapeutic components, including mindfulness exercises, goal-setting activities, journaling, mood tracking, and educational content related to mental health and coping strategies. This clinical trial evaluates the effectiveness, usability, and acceptability of the application when used as a self-guided mental wellness intervention among college students.

The study examines multiple forms of data, including behavioral change measures, user engagement metrics, usability assessments, and participant feedback, to assess the app's utility in supporting well-being. It is hypothesized that participants who use the application will demonstrate increased well-being compared to a control group, along with higher engagement and acceptability of the app-based intervention modality."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Well-Being, Psychological"],"keywords":["Digital Mental Health","College Students","Well-being"]},"designModule":{"studyType":"INTERVENTIONAL","phases":["NA"],"designInfo":{"allocation":"RANDOMIZED","interventionModel":"PARALLEL","primaryPurpose":"SUPPORTIVE_CARE","maskingInfo":{"masking":"SINGLE","whoMasked":["PARTICIPANT"]}},"enrollmentInfo":{"count":160,"type":"ESTIMATED"}},"armsInterventionsModule":{"armGroups":[{"label":"Control Group","type":"NO_INTERVENTION","description":"Group 1 will not use the app at all."},{"label":"App-intervention group","type":"EXPERIMENTAL","description":"Group 2 will use the mental health app almost every day for 4 weeks. This study involved 36 Cystic Fibrosis patients: 24 treated and 12 controls.","detailedDescription":"ROSCO-CF is a phase II, dose ranging, multicenter, double-blind, placebo controlled study to evaluate safety and effects of (R)-roscovitine in subjects with Cystic Fibrosis carrying 2 Cystic Fibrosis causing mutations with at least one F508del-CFTR mutation and chronically infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

The aim of this study is to assess the safety of increasing doses of roscovitine administered orally for 4 cycles of 4 consecutive days (treatment "on") separated by a 3 days treatment free period (treatment "off") in 36 adult cystic fibrosis subjects.

These 36 patients will be allocated to 3 groups of 12 subjects who will be randomized in a 2:1 ratio (active drug to matching placebo). In each group, 8 patients will receive roscovitine (200 mg, 400 mg, 2 X 400 mg in group 1, 2 and 3, respectively) and 4 will receive a matching placebo. Treatment will be provided by oral administration of capsules. Each patient will receive the same treatment throughout the 28 day study.

This phase II trial will give some preliminary information about safety and hints of effects of a new experimental treatment. If the data suggest that a short term treatment with roscovitine provides a safe, effective and convenient approach for CF patients chronically infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, patients participating in this proof of concept trial will be offered to participate in further longer term studies."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Cystic Fibrosis"],"keywords":["Cystic Fibrosis","Roscovitine","Seliciclib","CYC202"]},"designModule":{"studyType":"INTERVENTIONAL","phases":["PHASE2"],"designInfo":{"allocation":"RANDOMIZED","interventionModel":"PARALLEL","primaryPurpose":"TREATMENT","maskingInfo":{"masking":"TRIPLE","whoMasked":["PARTICIPANT","CARE_PROVIDER","INVESTIGATOR"]}},"enrollmentInfo":{"count":49,"type":"ACTUAL"}},"armsInterventionsModule":{"armGroups":[{"label":"Group 1","type":"EXPERIMENTAL","description":"200 mg roscovitine (8) or placebo (4) once daily for 4 cycles of 7 days (4 days "on" and 3 days "off")","interventionNames":["Drug: Roscovitine","Drug: Placebo"]},{"label":"Group 2","type":"EXPERIMENTAL","description":"400 mg roscovitine (8) or placebo (4) once daily for 4 cycles of 7 days (4 days "on" and 3 days "off")","interventionNames":["Drug: Roscovitine","Drug: Placebo"]},{"label":"Group 3","type":"EXPERIMENTAL","description":"400 mg roscovitine (8) or (4) placebo twice daily for cycles of 7 days (4 days "on" and 3 days "off")","interventionNames":["Drug: Roscovitine","Drug: Placebo"]}],"interventions":[{"type":"DRUG","name":"Roscovitine","description":"Roscovitine is an experimental drug candidate in the family of pharmacological cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitors that preferentially inhibit multiple enzyme targets including CDK2, CDK7 and CDK9. Findings aim to inform future public health screening policies.","detailedDescription":"This joint study by the City University of Hong Kong (CityU) and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) investigates the impact of preventive ovarian reserve screening and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled health counseling on reproductive anxiety and family planning intentions among women in Hong Kong.

Hong Kong currently faces record-low fertility rates. While the government has implemented various financial subsidies and tax incentives, these measures fail to address the underlying psychological barriers and medical uncertainties surrounding biological clocks. To address this gap, the study employs a 2 x 2 quasi-experimental design using propensity score matching and RCT applied to evaluate 660 nulliparous women aged 25 to 38 years:

* Intervention Group (n = 300): Participants receive an Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) blood test to quantify ovarian reserve. Results are delivered either through an interactive, culturally tailored AI conversational agent named "Shelby" (Group 2A) or a traditional static PDF laboratory report (Group 2B).
* Control Group (n = 300): Participants receive standard reproductive health education without biomarker testing, comparing interactive AI engagement (Group 1A) against standard educational brochures (Group 1B).

Key outcome measures evaluated at baseline and at a 2- to 4-week follow-up include medical comprehension accuracy, psychological distress assessed via the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-6), patient enablement (PEI), willingness to pay, and long-term fertility intentions. Strict ethical safeguards and distress protocols are integrated to automatically escalate any acute psychological distress to professional counselors. The findings will provide empirical evidence to support policy recommendations for territory-wide subsidized fertility screening in public healthcare."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Fertility Awareness","Ovarian Reserve","Family Planning"],"keywords":["Anti-Mullerian Hormon","Ovarian Reserve Screening","Family Planning"]},"designModule":{"studyType":"INTERVENTIONAL","phases":["NA"],"designInfo":{"allocation":"RANDOMIZED","interventionModel":"FACTORIAL","interventionModelDescription":"Primary Arm 1 (AMH Testing, n = 300):

The data collection procedure consisted of the following steps:

Baseline assessment: Participants first completed the socio-demographic section of the Patient Information Form, and the responses were recorded by the researcher.

Pre-intervention vein assessment: A tourniquet was applied to the patient's upper extremity, and vein characteristics were assessed by the nurse using the Vein Rating Scale (VRS) and the Vein Assessment Tool (VAT). During this assessment, no manoeuvres intended to enhance vein visibility (e.g., repeated hand opening and closing, tapping, or slapping the vein) were permitted after tourniquet application. The tourniquet was then removed, and the patient rested for 10 minutes before baseline (pre-test) measurements were recorded.

Intervention: Participants received one of the study interventions according to their assigned group.

Isometric exercise group: Participants were provided with silicone hand exercise balls and instructed to squeeze and release the ball 15-20 times.

Dry heat application group: A chemical gel compress heated to 40 ± 2°C was applied to the selected extremity. Based on previous evidence, maintaining local heat at 40 ± 2°C for at least 5 minutes is sufficient to induce vasodilation.

Control group: Participants received routine peripheral intravenous catheterisation care without any additional intervention.

Post-intervention vein assessment: Immediately after completion of the intervention, a tourniquet was reapplied, and vein characteristics were reassessed by the nurse using the VRS and VAT. These measurements constituted the post-test assessment.

Phase II clinical trials test the safety and effectiveness of an investigational regimen, IDR, to learn whether IDR works in treating a specific cancer. "Investigational" means that IDR is still being studied and that research doctors are trying to find out more about it-such as the safest dose to use, the side effects it may cause, and if IDR is effective for treating different types of cancer. It also means that the FDA (the U.S. Food and Drug Administration) has not yet approved IDR for use in participants with your type of cancer.

Ixazomib is a drug that may kill or stop cancer cells from growing by blocking the proteasome within the cell, which is responsible for degrading or breaking down a variety of proteins. This type of drug is called a proteasome inhibitor.

Rituximab is a type of protein called an antibody that attacks the cluster of differentiation 20 (CD20), a protein found on B-cells like WM. Rituximab is approved by the FDA for treating non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). Dexamethasone is a steroid and is similar to the hormones naturally produced by the adrenal glands; it prevents the release of substances that cause inflammation. Rituximab and dexamethasone are often used to treat WM, alone or in combination with other drugs. Combinations with rituximab, dexamethasone and other proteasome inhibitors have shown good response rates in WM participants. Ixazomib is a proteasome inhibitor; thus the investigator swill investigate if the combination of Ixazomib, Rituximab, and Dexamethasone is also active in WM.

In this research study, the investigators are combining a new treatment ixazomib with a standard regimen, rituximab and dexamethasone, to determine whether this combination (IDR) is effective and safe for participants with previously untreated WM."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Waldenstrom's Macroglobulinemia"],"keywords":["Waldenstrom's Macroglobulinemia"]},"designModule":{"studyType":"INTERVENTIONAL","phases":["PHASE2"],"designInfo":{"allocation":"NA","interventionModel":"SINGLE_GROUP","primaryPurpose":"TREATMENT","maskingInfo":{"masking":"NONE"}},"enrollmentInfo":{"count":26,"type":"ACTUAL"}},"armsInterventionsModule":{"armGroups":[{"label":"IDR","type":"EXPERIMENTAL","description":"\- IDR The study treatment will consist on an induction and a maintenance phase. 1. Participant is at least 18 years of age
2. Participant must provide written informed consent prior to any study procedures
3. Participant must have a clinical diagnosis of NF1
4. Participant has 10 clinically diagnosed Target cNFs with preferably 2 Target cNFs located on the face and 8 Target cNFs located on the anterior trunk or upper extremities. Alternatively, at least 1 Target cNF is located on the face, in which case 9 Target cNFs must be located on the anterior trunk or upper extremities. Each Target cNF must meet the following criteria:

   * Has, in the investigator's opinion, a clinically typical appearance
   * Is not within 1 centimeter (cm) of the orbital rim
   * Is not covered with hair that might, in the investigator's opinion, interfere with obtaining photographs or impair evaluation of the cNF
   * Has a Physician's Tumor Assessment grade ≥2
   * Is dome shaped
   * Is not pedunculated
   * Is a discrete cNF surrounded by sufficient non-affected skin that, in the investigator's opinion:
   * The dimensions can be measured
   * The perimeter can be outlined in the study photographs
   * Is not irritated (or example, bleeding, inflamed)
   * Is not in an area participant to repeated trauma (or example, area that is shaved, on the beltline, under a bra strap, etc.)
   * Does not have an active cutaneous infection
   * Target cNFs on the face must have the following tumor dimensions:
   * Has a length that is ≥5 millimeters (mm) and ≤14 mm
   * Has a width that is ≥5 mm and ≤14 mm
   * Has a height that is ≥2 mm.
   * Target cNFs on the anterior trunk or upper extremities must have the following tumor dimensions:
   * Has a length that is ≥ 7mm and ≤14 mm
   * Has a width that is ≥5 mm and ≤14 mm
   * Has a height that is ≥2 mm.
5. Participant agrees to avoid exposure of Target cNFs to excessive sunlight and to use her/his routine sunscreen if excessive exposure cannot be avoided
6. Participant agrees not to use tanning beds
7. Participant is willing to forego treatment of each Target cNF, except protocol specified therapy, during the study
8. Female participants who are women of childbearing potential must have a negative urine pregnancy test result and be willing to use a protocol approved, contraceptive method for the duration of the study
9. Participant is willing and able to follow all study instructions and to attend all study visits.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Participant has used any of the following topical therapies within the specified period prior to Visit 1 (screening visit) on or in proximity to any Target cNF that, in the investigator's opinion, impairs evaluation of any the cNFs or which exposes the participant to an unacceptable risk by study participation:

   * Corticosteroids; 30 days
   * Prescription retinoids (for example, tazarotene, tretinoin, adapalene); 30 days
   * \> 5% of an alpha-hydroxy acid (for example, glycolic acid, lactic acid); 30 days
   * Fluorouracil; 30 days
   * Imiquimod; 30 days
   * LASER, light (for example, intense pulsed light \[IPL\], photo-dynamic therapy \[PDT\]) or other energy-based therapy; 180 days
   * Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MEK) inhibitor or V-Raf Murine Sarcoma Viral Oncogene Homolog B (BRAF) inhibitor; ever.
2. The participant has used any of the following systemic medications therapies within the specified period prior to Visit 1 (screening visit):

   * Retinoids (for example, etretinate, isotretinoin); 90 days
   * MEK inhibitors; 180 days
   * BRAF inhibitors; 180 days
3. Participant has a history of hypersensitivity to any of the ingredients in the study medications
4. Participant has any known intercurrent illness or physical condition that would, in the investigator's opinion, impair evaluation of a Target cNF or which exposes the participant to an unacceptable risk by study participation
5. Participant has, in the investigator's opinion, clinically relevant history of liver disease, including viral hepatitis, current alcohol abuse, or cirrhosis
6. Participant has a history of metastatic disease, or active cancer (excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer, Stage I cervical cancer, ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast, or Stage 0 chronic lymphocytic lymphoma) within the previous 5 years
7. Participant has any condition (for example, other skin conditions or diseases, metabolic dysfunction, physical examination findings, clinical laboratory findings) or situation (for example, vacation, scheduled surgery) that would, in the investigator's opinion, impair evaluation of a Target cNF or which exposes the participant to an unacceptable risk by study participation
8. However, there are very few prospective studies conducted in real clinical settings directed at patients seeking healthcare for assessment of skin lesions, and nosuch studies at all in primary care, where the majority of patients are managed.

Project aim: To study the accuracy, reliability, and clinical utility of an AI-based decision support system (Dermalyser), developed for primary care, in distinguishing skin cancer from benign lesions.

Method: Cluster-randomized controlled trial at approx. 30 primary care centers in Sweden, Germany, Scotland, the Netherlands and Australia. At study start, the participating primary care centres in each country are equally randomised to either be enabled to use the Dermalyser (intervention phase) or to assess patients according to the standard clinical procedure (control phase). When half of the intended sample size (i.e. 1500 of 3000 participants) have been included, the primary care centres switch phase from intervention to control, or vice versa. During the intervention phase, the physicians may use (if found indicated) Dermalyser as a part of their clinical evaluation, whereas during the control phase the physicians follow their ordinary diagnostic routine without support from Dermalyser. This will direct the participants to either an intervention or a control cohort. Both groups will be followed for up to 5 years, with regard to the tumour diagnoses, proportions of skin cancer/benign lesions, and morbidity and mortality in skin cancer. Possible between-group differences will be investigated statistically.
